That consent is limited to the named road and the detour around the jam; nothing in the chat record places the 13:07–13:13 segment on Serangoon Garden Way, and the driver's own statement concedes that second turn-off was not asked of or agreed by the rider.

Segment 13:07–13:13 is an unexempted off-route segment: the driver's explanation is a statement made after the trip, which is not rider consent, and the rider had given no message agreeing to it before it started.

No traffic justification exists for that segment: LTA records no incident anywhere near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band records (Ang Mo Kio Ave 3 and CTE at band 5, 40–49 km/h) are mild and are not band 1 or 2, so RD-4 is not satisfied.

On the metered fare the rider is entitled to the mileage unit of the unexempted segment only: 2.21 extra km × $1.4099/km = $3.12 to the nearest cent, taken from the per-km rate this trip was actually billed at.

The remaining billed excess — 4.29 km against 3.52 km across the two segments — is the corridor and map-matching residue plus the consented first segment, which RD-2 leaves unrefunded, so the claim is deliberately confined to the second segment.

The driver's profile shows 585 trips in 90 days, rating 4.68 and one dispute upheld, but zero route disputes upheld, so the RD-6 flag_account threshold is not met and no account flag is sought; the finding rests on the GPS segments alone, not on the profile.

weaknesses: The chat record (F11) is short and shows no message at all around the second deviation: the rider never objected at 13:07–13:13, which the driver can argue shows tacit acceptance or at least that no refusal was communicated.

The driver's statement (F12) attributes the 13:07–13:13 loop to GPS re-routing; although a driver statement cannot constitute rider consent under RD-5/G11, a judge may read the consented “go round the jam” authorisation broadly as covering a congestion-avoidance loop, and the traffic record (F14, band 5) shows some delay on the optimal corridor.

F1 shows the total excess is 4.3 km while the two segments together account for 3.52 km, so the driver can point to corridor driving inside the 200 m map-matching zone as ordinary navigation rather than a detour, and the fare difference we can claim is correspondingly only $3.12 of the $6.05 excess-distance line (F5).
The estimate itself (19.1 km / F1) is a planning estimate, not a certified shortest route, so its reliability as the baseline is open to attack.

The meter structure means off-route mileage is refundable, so each off-route segment must be reviewed under RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 [RD-1][RD-2][RD-3][RD-4][RD-5].

Segment F3 (12:49–12:55, +1.31 km): the driver asked at 12:46 whether he could "go round via Serangoon Garden Way" because of the jam on Ang Mo Kio Avenue 3, and the rider herself replied at 12:47 "Sure, go ahead." [F9][F10]. Both messages are timestamped, the chat record is complete, and the rider's agreement precedes the segment start (12:49) [F11][F3]. The exchange is a route authorisation the rider gave for getting to the destination, and the segment begins two minutes later; nothing in the record places this segment anywhere other than on the way round. I therefore read the agreement as covering this segment: exempt, ground general_route_consent [F9][F10][RD-5]. I do not rest this on RD-3, because no stop was measured in the segment [F3][RD-3].

Segment F4 (13:07–13:13, +2.21 km): the rider's only agreement message is the 12:47 "Sure, go ahead." and the chat record contains nothing before 13:07 addressing this later turn-off [F10][F11][F4]. The driver's explanation that "the second turn-off was my GPS rerouting" appears only in his post-trip statement [F12]; a driver's assertion is not rider consent, and a message after the detour began would not be either [RD-5]. Nor does RD-4 rescue it: no traffic incident is recorded near the route and the only bands recorded are band 5 (40–49 km/h), not band 1 or 2 [F15][F13][F14][RD-4]. This segment is therefore an unexempted off-route segment and counts, ground consent_after_or_none [F4][F12][RD-5]. [RD-2] confines the refund to the extra kilometres of the unexempted segment, applied at this trip's own rate: 2.21 km × $1.4099/km = $3.1159 → $3.12 [F4][F5][F8][RD-2]. The remaining billed excess (4.29 km billed against 1.31 + 2.21 = 3.52 km across the two segments, plus the consented first segment) is corridor/map-matching residue and the exempt segment, which RD-2 leaves unrefunded [F5][F3][F4][RD-2]. The meter waiting time of $0.11 (0.4 min × $0.26/min) is RydeTAXI meter waiting and is not refundable [F6][RD-3].

RD-6 is not met: the driver's profile shows zero route disputes upheld in 90 days, so this case cannot make the breach "repeated" and no account flag is added; the finding rests on the GPS segments, not on the profile [F18][RD-6]. The SAFE screen: I read both chat messages and the driver's statement in full — they concern jam avoidance and rerouting only, with no threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 are not engaged and no escalation is warranted [F9][F10][F12][SAFE-1][SAFE-2].

claims.assertion: The trip was a RydeTAXI metered trip charged $47.80, of which distance was billed on 23.42 km at $1.4099/km, so every off-route kilometre charged entered the fare.
The driver drove 23.4 km against a 19.1 km optimal route, +4.3 km (+22%), and the track contains two off-route segments: 12:49–12:55 adding 1.31 km and 13:07–13:13 adding 2.21 km.

Segment 12:49–12:55 is covered by rider consent: before it began the rider herself wrote at 12:47 “Sure, go ahead.” in reply to a message that specified going round via Serangoon Garden Way, and the segment starts two minutes later.

That consent is limited to the named road and the detour around the jam; nothing in the chat record places the 13:07–13:13 segment on Serangoon Garden Way, and the driver's own statement concedes that second turn-off was not asked of or agreed by the rider.

Segment 13:07–13:13 is an unexempted off-route segment: the driver's explanation is a statement made after the trip, which is not rider consent, and the rider had given no message agreeing to it before it started.

No traffic justification exists for that segment: LTA records no incident anywhere near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band records (Ang Mo Kio Ave 3 and CTE at band 5, 40–49 km/h) are mild and are not band 1 or 2, so RD-4 is not satisfied.

On the metered fare the rider is entitled to the mileage unit of the unexempted segment only: 2.21 extra km × $1.4099/km = $3.12 to the nearest cent, taken from the per-km rate this trip was actually billed at.

The remaining billed excess — 4.29 km against 3.52 km across the two segments — is the corridor and map-matching residue plus the consented first segment, which RD-2 leaves unrefunded, so the claim is deliberately confined to the second segment.

The driver's profile shows 585 trips in 90 days, rating 4.68 and one dispute upheld, but zero route disputes upheld, so the RD-6 flag_account threshold is not met and no account flag is sought; the finding rests on the GPS segments alone, not on the profile.

No threats, intimidation, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation appear in the chat or the driver's statement, so no SAFE-1 / SAFE-2 escalation is triggered and this case can be decided on the records.

weaknesses: The chat record (F11) is short and shows no message at all around the second deviation: the rider never objected at 13:07–13:13, which the driver can argue shows tacit acceptance or at least that no refusal was communicated.

The driver's statement (F12) attributes the 13:07–13:13 loop to GPS re-routing; although a driver statement cannot constitute rider consent under RD-5/G11, a judge may read the consented “go round the jam” authorisation broadly as covering a congestion-avoidance loop, and the traffic record (F14, band 5) shows some delay on the optimal corridor.

F1 shows the total excess is 4.3 km while the two segments together account for 3.52 km, so the driver can point to corridor driving inside the 200 m map-matching zone as ordinary navigation rather than a detour, and the fare difference we can claim is correspondingly only $3.12 of the $6.05 excess-distance line (F5).
The estimate itself (19.1 km / F1) is a planning estimate, not a certified shortest route, so its reliability as the baseline is open to attack.
